questions.q: If an application forgets the sp_set_session_context call that sets TenantId before querying a vector table protected by an RLS policy, what happens?
options: The query returns all tenants' rows as a fallback
SQL Server raises an error and blocks the query
The query returns zero rows - fail-closed by design
The query returns rows but logs a warning
questions.explain: The chapter states that forgetting sp_set_session_context makes the query return zero rows: the predicate function compares TenantId to the session context, which is NULL, so nothing matches - fail-closed by design.

questions.q: When an RLS tenant predicate applies after a DiskANN ANN scan, the chapter recommends which workaround to preserve recall?
options: Over-fetch 10-20x the final k with TOP_N, then filter in the outer query
Drop the RLS predicate for ANN queries and filter in the application
Reduce the DiskANN M parameter to lower candidate counts
Disable the vector index entirely for multi-tenant tables
questions.explain: Because the filter applies after the ANN index returns candidates, only a few may belong to the tenant, collapsing effective recall. The fix is tenant-safe over-fetch: 10-20x the final k via TOP_N, filtered in the outer query, measuring recall@k per tenant.

questions.q: What is the chapter's hierarchy of tenant-isolation assurance, from strongest to weakest?
options: RLS predicates, then namespaces, then separate indexes
Mandatory metadata filters, then separate indexes, then RLS
API key scoping, then namespaces, then RLS
Separate indexes per tenant, then namespaces/tenant-shards, then mandatory metadata filters, then RLS predicates
questions.explain: The chapter ranks isolation strength: separate indexes per tenant (structural, strongest) > namespaces/tenant-shards > mandatory metadata filters > RLS predicates, choosing based on tenant count and isolation requirements.

questions.q: What is the chapter's critical rule about enforcing document-level permissions on vector retrieval?
options: Filter in application code after retrieval to keep SQL simple
Enforce permissions before retrieval in the database query, never after
Permissions only matter at ingest time, not query time
Re-rank first with the LLM, then remove unauthorized chunks
questions.explain: The rule is enforce permissions before retrieval, never after: post-retrieval filtering is both a security hole (the LLM already saw the text if you re-rank first) and a quality bug (you return fewer than k results).

questions.q: Why does the chapter say embeddings are not anonymized data?
options: A vector preserves enough semantic content that sensitive text can be partially reconstructed, so the vector store carries the source documents' classification
Embeddings can be decrypted with the database master key
Vector indexes store plaintext copies by default
TDE does not apply to VECTOR columns
questions.explain: The chapter warns that a vector is a compressed semantic fingerprint preserving enough content for partial reconstruction - and the chunk text alongside it is the original sensitive content in full - so the store must be treated with the source documents' classification, with PII scrubbing before embedding.
